Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

derivations.claim: Let $\delta_h(t)=u_{\theta_0+h}(t)-u_{\theta_0}(t)$. Differentiability of $u_0$ gives $\|u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)\|_2\le C_0\|h\|_2$ for small $h$. Subtract the Volterra equations [F1] and apply [F2] on the segment between $(u_{\theta_0+h}(t),\theta_0+h)$ and $(u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. Boundedness of $D f$ on $O$ gives $$\|\delta_h(t)\|_2\le C_0\|h\|_2+L\int_0^t(\|\delta_h(s)\|_2+\|h\|_2)\,ds.$$ Since $t\le T$, [F3] yields $\sup_t\|\delta_h(t)\|_2\le(C_0+LT)e^{LT}\|h\|_2$.

Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and let $B_j(t)$ be column $j$ of $D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. For each parameter coordinate $j$, the augmented vector $Z_j=(S_{\cdot j},1)$ solves the homogeneous linear system $$Z_j'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}A(t)&B_j(t)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Z_j(t),\qquad Z_j(0)=\begin{pmatrix}D u_0(\theta_0)_{\cdot j}\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Embed $Z_j(0)$ as one column of a square $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ initial matrix, with all other columns zero. The unique linear matrix solution supplied by [F5] has that vector solution as the selected column. Thus the tangent equation has a unique solution for each of the finitely many columns.

Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and $B(t)=D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$, and define $\rho_h(t)=f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t)+\delta_h(t),\theta_0+h)-f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)-A(t)\delta_h(t)-B(t)h$. Uniform continuity of $D f$ on $\overline O$ and the integral remainder along the secant give $\sup_t\|\rho_h(t)\|_2=o(\|h\|_2)$, since step 1.1 gives $\sup_t(\|\delta_h(t)\|_2+\|h\|_2)=O(\|h\|_2)$. Also $u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)=D u_0(\theta_0)h+o(\|h\|_2)$.

Let $E_h(t)=\delta_h(t)-S(t)h$, and let $r_0(h)=u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)-D u_0(\theta_0)h$. The Volterra equations and the field remainder $\rho_h$ from step 2.1 give $E_h(t)=r_0(h)+\int_0^t\bigl(A(s)E_h(s)+\rho_h(s)\bigr)ds$, where $A(s)=D_u f(s,u_{\theta_0}(s),\theta_0)$. By [F4], $\|E_h(t)\|_2\le\|r_0(h)\|_2+T\sup_s\|\rho_h(s)\|_2+L\int_0^t\|E_h(s)\|_2ds$. Both first terms are $o(\|h\|_2)$ by step 2.1 and differentiability of $u_0$. Applying [F3] yields $\sup_t\|E_h(t)\|_2=o(\|h\|_2)$. Thus the Fréchet derivative at $\theta_0$ exists and equals $S$.

For any sequence $\theta_j\to\theta_0$ in $V_\theta$, step 1.1 gives $u_{\theta_j}\to u_{\theta_0}$ uniformly, and uniform continuity of $D f$ on $\overline O$ makes the tangent coefficients $A_j,B_j$ converge uniformly to $A,B$. Subtracting the tangent integral equations gives $S_j(t)-S(t)=D u_0(\theta_j)-D u_0(\theta_0)+\int_0^t\bigl(A_j(s)(S_j(s)-S(s))+(A_j(s)-A(s))S(s)+B_j(s)-B(s)\bigr)ds$. The initial and coefficient differences tend to zero, while $A_j$ are uniformly bounded; [F3] then gives $\|S_j-S\|_{C([0,T])}\to0$. Since $\theta_0$ is arbitrary in $V_\theta$, the derivative is continuous throughout that set, so the flow map is $C^1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

Input a graph from [[def-finite-straight-line-computational-program]] and an admissible point $x$. Evaluate and store all primal values in topological order. Initialize every operation cotangent and every input cotangent to zero. Seed the scalar output by setting its cotangent to $1$: if $o$ is an operation, set $\bar z_o=1$; if $o$ is input coordinate $i$, set $\bar x_i=1$. For $j=T,T-1,\ldots,1$, and for every parent slot $k=1,\ldots,r_j$, compute the contribution
$$c_{j,k}=D_k\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})^T\bar z_j$$
and add it to the cotangent accumulator of that parent: use $\bar x_i$ if the parent is input coordinate $i$, and $\bar z_\ell$ if it is operation node $\ell$. If the same parent node occurs in multiple slots, add every slot contribution. Return the scalar output $f(x)$ and the input cotangents $(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n)$ as the Euclidean gradient. A point outside the admissible domain returns DOMAIN_ERROR; a branch boundary or ambiguous active branch returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. The procedure differentiates the real-arithmetic graph; it makes no floating-point error claim.

For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By the chain rule [F4] applied to $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$, $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$; differentiating the initial map gives $S_0=Dx_0(\theta)$. These are the forward tangent equations for this finite composition.

Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. By [F3], reverse mode returns the exact derivative of this finite C1 graph.

Differentiate the objective in [F1] using the forward sensitivities in step 1.1. The chain rule gives $$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S_N^TD_x\phi^T+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(D_\theta\ell_n^T+S_n^TD_x\ell_n^T).$$ This is the direct tangent expression, with all derivatives evaluated along the trajectory.

The adjoint equation gives $p_n^TS_n=D_x\ell_nS_n+p_{n+1}^TA_nS_n$. Since $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$, rearranging yields $$D_x\ell_nS_n=p_n^TS_n-p_{n+1}^TS_{n+1}+p_{n+1}^TB_n.$$ Summing over $n$ telescopes; $p_N=D_x\phi^T$ cancels the terminal tangent term in step 2.1 and leaves $S_0^Tp_0+\sum_n B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Adding the direct parameter derivatives from step 2.1 gives the displayed adjoint formula.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. Then the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$.

derivations.claim: By [F3], the terminal linear adjoint equation has a unique $C^1$ solution on $[0,T]$.

By [F1], the state depends $C^1$ on the parameter and has sensitivity $S$. The chain rule gives the column gradient of the running integrand as $D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+S(t)^TD_u\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T$. The mean-value integral formula, boundedness and uniform continuity of the objective derivatives on the common compact tube, and the uniform first-order state remainder from [F1] make the running first-order remainder $o(\|h\|)$ uniformly in $t$ for a parameter increment $h$. Integration therefore gives its derivative by integrating that column gradient. The terminal chain rule gives $D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T$. Consequently $\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T+\int_0^T(D_\theta\ell^T+S^TD_u\ell^T)\,dt$.

Let $d,s\ge1$, $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{s\times s}$, $b,c\in\mathbb R^s$, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be a vector field on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). For an initial state $y\in\mathbb R^d$ and time $t$ with $(t,y)\in D$, and a step $h>0$, a stage vector $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_s)\in(\mathbb R^d)^s$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,Y_j)\in D$ for every $j$. An admissible vector solves

$$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j),\qquad i=1,\ldots,s.$$

When a solution $Y$ is selected, the method update is

$$\Psi_h(t,y)=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_i f(t+c_ih,Y_i).$$

On the admissible stage set, the **stage update residual** is the vector with blocks

$$G_i(Y)=Y_i-y-h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j).$$

The associated stage derivative residual is $G(Y)/h$. The tableau is **stiffly accurate** when $b_j=a_{sj}$ for all $j$ and $c_s=1$; in that case the last stage $Y_s$ equals the method update. The equations may have no, one, or several solutions in a proposed branch set; this definition alone asserts no solvability.

Let $m,d\ge1$, $h>0$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, and centers $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(\mathbb R^d)^m$. On block vectors define

$$\|Y\|_{\infty,2}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|Y_i\|_2,\qquad \|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_{j=1}^m|a_{ij}|.$$

Let $F:\mathcal B\to(\mathbb R^d)^m$, with components $F_i:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R^d$, be defined on the closed product ball $\mathcal B=\{Y:\|Y-c\|_{\infty,2}\le R\}$, where $R>0$. Suppose constants $M,L\ge0$ satisfy, for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal B$,

$$\|F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le M,\qquad \|F(Y)-F(Z)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Y-Z\|_{\infty,2},$$

and $h\|A\|_\infty M\le R$, $q:=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$. Define $\Phi(Y)=c+h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ and $G(Y)=Y-\Phi(Y)$. Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $Y^*\in\mathcal B$, equivalently $G(Y^*)=0$. Every approximate stage vector $\widetilde Y\in\mathcal B$ satisfies

$$\|\widetilde Y-Y^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|G(\widetilde Y)\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$

If the derivative-scaled stage residual is $r=G(\widetilde Y)/h$, the right side is $h\|r\|_{\infty,2}/(1-q)$. The hypotheses $h\|A\|_\infty L<1$ and the invariant-ball bound are local solvability conditions; this result gives no global branch outside $\mathcal B$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.

derivations.claim: For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, apply [F1] to $a_\theta$ and $\ell_\theta$; this gives a unique $u_\theta$ and the bound $\|u_\theta\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\|\ell_\theta\|_{V^*}$. Since $\ell_\theta$ is continuous, these state norms are locally bounded in $\theta$.

For sufficiently small $h$ with $\theta+h\in\Theta_0$, put $\delta u=u_{\theta+h}-u_\theta$, $\delta A=A_{\theta+h}-A_\theta$, and $\delta\ell=\ell_{\theta+h}-\ell_\theta$. Subtract the two variational equations to get $a_\theta(\delta u,v)=\delta\ell(v)-(\delta A\,u_{\theta+h})(v)$. Taking $v=\delta u$, using coercivity and the dual norm, and dividing by $\|\delta u\|_V$ when it is nonzero gives $\|\delta u\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\bigl(\|\delta\ell\|_{V^*}+\|\delta A\|\,\|u_{\theta+h}\|_V\bigr)=O(\|h\|_2)$. The same bound is immediate when $\delta u=0$. Thus the state map is locally Lipschitz.

For each direction $h\in\mathbb R^m$, define $w_h$ by $a_\theta(w_h,v)=D\ell_\theta[h](v)-\bigl(DA_\theta[h]u_\theta\bigr)(v)$. The right side is a bounded linear functional, so [F1] gives a unique $w_h$. Uniqueness and linearity of the right side in $h$ show $h\mapsto w_h$ is linear.

Write $\delta\ell=D\ell_\theta[h]+r_\ell$ and $\delta A=DA_\theta[h]+r_A$, where $\|r_\ell\|+\|r_A\|=o(\|h\|_2)$ by [F2]. Subtract the equation for $w_h$ in step 2.2 from the state-difference equation in step 2.1. With $e_h=\delta u-w_h$, this gives $a_\theta(e_h,v)=r_\ell(v)-(r_Au_\theta)(v)-(DA_\theta[h]\delta u)(v)-(r_A\delta u)(v)$. The first two terms have dual norm $o(\|h\|_2)$; the last two have that order because $\|DA_\theta[h]\|=O(\|h\|_2)$, $\|r_A\|=o(\|h\|_2)$, and $\|\delta u\|_V=O(\|h\|_2)$ by step 2.1. Coercivity yields $\|e_h\|_V=o(\|h\|_2)$, proving Fréchet differentiability and the stated derivative equation.

The solution operator $A_\theta^{-1}:V^*\to V$ has norm at most $\alpha^{-1}$. For nearby $\theta,\widetilde\theta$, the identity $A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}-A_\theta^{-1} =A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}(A_\theta-A_{\widetilde\theta})A_\theta^{-1}$ shows its operator-norm continuity. The formula in step 2.2, together with continuity of $u_\theta$, $D A_\theta$, and $D\ell_\theta$, then shows $D_\theta u_\theta$ is continuous. Hence the state map is $C^1$.

in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. In the **exact variational problem**, $V$ is a Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded coercive sesquilinear form (bilinear when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$), linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ is bounded and has the same linearity in its test argument as the second argument of $a$. Exact solutions satisfy $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in V$. Boundedness and coercivity have the meanings in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]].

For a **conforming perturbed Galerkin problem**, $V_h\subseteq V$ is a finite-dimensional subspace, $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ are the discrete form and load, and $u_h\in V_h$ solves $a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$. $$\delta_{a,h}(v_h):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|a(v_h,w_h)-a_h(v_h,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V},\qquad \delta_{F,h}:=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F(w_h)-F_h(w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_V}.$$

If $V_h=\{0\}$, both defects are defined to be zero. The load defect $\delta_{F,h}$ includes any source approximation or data oscillation; it is not assumed small or zero without a separate bound.

For a **nonconforming problem**, the exact space $V$ and finite-dimensional trial space $V_h$ need not satisfy $V_h\subseteq V$. Put $X_h:=V+V_h$ and equip it with a norm $\|\cdot\|_h$ whose restrictions to $V$ and $V_h$ are norms. $$\delta^{\mathrm{nc}}_h(u):=\sup_{w_h\in V_h\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|}{\|w_h\|_h},$$

[[thm-aubin-nitsche-l2-error-estimate-under-adjoint-regularity]]. Suppose
there are $s\in(0,1]$, a normed regularity space $R_s\subseteq V$ for $z_e$,

$$\|z_e\|_{R_s}\le C_R\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
$$\inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|z_e-w_h\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_D h^s\|z_e\|_{R_s}.$$

$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le \frac{M^2}{\alpha}C_{\rm FE}C_DC_R h^{r+s}|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Here $C_{\rm FE}$ is the primal interpolation constant and $M,\alpha$ are

branch, one may take $R_1=H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$ with the $H^2$ norm,

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

about one $x$ at a time.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a separable real Hilbert space and $Y$ a real Hilbert space, and
let $u\in H^1(0,T;X)$ (meaning
$u,u'\in L^2(0,T;X)$ with distribution derivative). It has a unique
continuous representative on $[0,T]$. Let
$P\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ be a fixed bounded linear map. Then
$Pu\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and $(Pu)'=Pu'$.

If instead $P:[0,T]\to\mathcal L(X,Y)$ is continuously differentiable in
operator norm, then $P(t)u(t)\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}(P(t)u(t))=P'(t)u(t)+P(t)u'(t)\quad\text{a.e.}$$
In particular, a differentiable time-dependent Ritz comparison contributes
the term $P'(t)u(t)$ to its residual derivative.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Every invertible matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb F)$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, has a unique factorisation

$$A=QR,$$

where $Q^*Q=I$ and $R$ is upper triangular with positive real diagonal entries. Thus $Q$ is orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ and unitary over $\mathbb C$. The assertion includes the unique $0\times0$ factorisation.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

The orthogonal operators on a finite-dimensional real inner product space form a group under composition, as do the unitary operators on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. Every such operator $T$ satisfies

$$|\det T|=1.$$

Over $\mathbb R$, this says $\det T\in\{-1,1\}$. In dimension zero, the unique determinant is $1$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: Induction on $k$ using $A_kQ_{k-1}=Q_kR_k$ gives $$P_kQ_0=Q_kR_kR_{k-1}\cdots R_1,\qquad P_k:=A_k\cdots A_1.$$ For $k=1$ this is the defining factorization; multiplying the identity at $k$ on the left by $A_{k+1}$ and substituting $A_{k+1}Q_k=Q_{k+1}R_{k+1}$ proves the next case.

Orthogonal factors preserve Euclidean norms, so $\sigma_{\min}(R_k)=\sigma_{\min}(Q_kR_k)=\sigma_{\min}(A_kQ_{k-1})=\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma$. For a fixed $i$, the leading $(i-1)\times(i-1)$ block of $R_k$ is invertible. Choose $x\in\mathbb R^{i-1}$ solving $R_{1:i-1,1:i-1}x=-R_{1:i-1,i}$ and set $z=(x,1,0,\ldots,0)^T$. Upper triangularity gives $R_kz=r_{k,ii}e_i$ and $\|z\|_2\ge1$, so $\sigma_{\min}(R_k)\le\|R_kz\|_2/\|z\|_2\le r_{k,ii}$. For $i=1$, take $z=e_1$. Hence $r_{k,ii}\ge\sigma$.

Take determinants in step 1.1. By [F2], $\det(P_N)\det(Q_0)=\det(Q_N)\prod_{k=1}^N\det(R_k)$. By [F3] each $\det(R_k)=\prod_i r_{k,ii}>0$, and by [F4] $|\det(Q_0)|=|\det(Q_N)|=1$. Thus $|\det(P_N)|=\prod_{k,i}r_{k,ii}$. Taking logarithms of positive numbers proves the exact identity.

Both $r_{k,ii}$ and $\widetilde r_{k,ii}$ are at least $\sigma/2$. By [F5], $|\log\widetilde r_{k,ii}-\log r_{k,ii}|\le(2/\sigma)|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|$. Adding the computation error $\delta_{k,i}$ and summing the scalar bounds by the triangle inequality proves the stated numerical log bound. The lower singular-value bound is essential to keep the log derivative bounded; if any factor is singular its determinant is zero and its log-volume is undefined.

Let $m,d\ge1$, $h>0$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, and centers $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(\mathbb R^d)^m$. On block vectors define

$$\|Y\|_{\infty,2}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|Y_i\|_2,\qquad \|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_{j=1}^m|a_{ij}|.$$

Let $F:\mathcal B\to(\mathbb R^d)^m$, with components $F_i:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R^d$, be defined on the closed product ball $\mathcal B=\{Y:\|Y-c\|_{\infty,2}\le R\}$, where $R>0$. Suppose constants $M,L\ge0$ satisfy, for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal B$,

$$\|F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le M,\qquad \|F(Y)-F(Z)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Y-Z\|_{\infty,2},$$

and $h\|A\|_\infty M\le R$, $q:=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$. Define $\Phi(Y)=c+h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ and $G(Y)=Y-\Phi(Y)$. Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $Y^*\in\mathcal B$, equivalently $G(Y^*)=0$. Every approximate stage vector $\widetilde Y\in\mathcal B$ satisfies

$$\|\widetilde Y-Y^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|G(\widetilde Y)\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$

If the derivative-scaled stage residual is $r=G(\widetilde Y)/h$, the right side is $h\|r\|_{\infty,2}/(1-q)$. The hypotheses $h\|A\|_\infty L<1$ and the invariant-ball bound are local solvability conditions; this result gives no global branch outside $\mathcal B$.

Let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ define a first-order initial-value problem on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$. Given a time $t_n$, step $h_n>0$, and state $y_n$ with $(t_n,y_n)\in D$, an admissible endpoint $y_{n+1}$ must satisfy $(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1})\in D$. $$y_{n+1}=y_n+h_n f(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1}).$$

$$G_n^{\rm BE}(z)=z-y_n-h_n f(t_n+h_n,z).$$

Assume Countable Choice and the elliptic state setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]] and [[lem-elliptic-state-map-c1-under-uniform-coercivity]]. Let $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For a parameter $\theta$, let $p_\theta\in V$ solve the adjoint variational problem
$$a_\theta(v,p_\theta)=D_uJ(u_\theta,\theta)[v]\qquad(v\in V).$$
Then the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$ is $C^1$ and
$$D_\theta j(\theta)[\eta]=D_\theta J(u_\theta,\theta)[\eta]+D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](p_\theta)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,p_\theta).$$
No symmetry of $a_\theta$ is required; the adjoint uses the transposed variational form displayed above.

Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and

$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in

[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the

denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$

axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The function $u(t)=e^{\theta t}s$ satisfies $u'=\theta u$ and $u(0)=s$, so uniqueness of the IVP identifies the exact interval flow with $\Phi_\tau(s,\theta)=e^{\tau\theta}s$. Let $A_1,\ldots,A_N\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be invertible, with $n,N\ge1$, and let $Q_0$ be orthogonal. For $1\le k\le N$, form the unique positive-diagonal QR factorization
$$A_kQ_{k-1}=Q_kR_k,$$
where $Q_k$ is orthogonal and $R_k$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal $r_{k,ii}$. Put $P_N=A_N\cdots A_1$ and define the exact finite-time log-volume change by $\log|\det P_N|$. Then
$$\log|\det P_N|=\sum_{k=1}^N\sum_{i=1}^n\log r_{k,ii}.$$
No infinite-time Lyapunov exponent or shadowing conclusion follows.

For a numerical log record, define $\sigma_{\min}(A):=\inf_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Ax\|_2$. If $\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma>0$, each exact $r_{k,ii}\ge\sigma$. If positive computed diagonals $\widetilde r_{k,ii}$ satisfy $|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|\le\varepsilon_{k,i}\le\sigma/2$, and each computed logarithm $\widehat l_{k,i}$ satisfies $|\widehat l_{k,i}-\log\widetilde r_{k,ii}|\le\delta_{k,i}$, then
$$\left|\sum_{k,i}\widehat l_{k,i}-\log|\det P_N|\right|\le\sum_{k,i}\left(\frac{2\varepsilon_{k,i}}{\sigma}+\delta_{k,i}\right).$$
If any factor loses rank, this log-volume branch returns failure.
